questions.q: Your code has a NewTask interface. Why is that not enough to check a request body?
questions.explain: TypeScript types disappear when the code is compiled. A request body arrives while the program runs, so you need a check that exists at runtime: a schema.
options: Because interfaces only work on classes, not on JSON
Types are removed before the program runs, so they cannot check data that arrives at runtime
Because TypeScript checks the body only in production
Because interfaces can only describe strings and numbers

questions.q: Why is it npm install @zudojs/schema @zudojs/errors, with no -D?
questions.explain: -D is for tools you only need while developing, like tsc or tsx. Schema and errors run inside your program, so they are normal dependencies.
options: Because -D only works for packages that start with @types/
Because ZudoJS packages refuse to install as dev dependencies
Your program needs them to run, so they are ordinary dependencies, not development tools
Because -D would install them globally on your computer

questions.q: You asked npm for two packages, and it added four. Why?
questions.explain: A package's own dependencies are installed with it. @zudojs/schema builds on a couple of smaller ZudoJS packages, so npm adds those for you.
options: @zudojs/schema uses two more small ZudoJS packages, and npm installs them too
npm always installs two copies of each package, one for Node and one for the browser
npm also added the TypeScript compiler and tsx
It is a mistake; you should uninstall the extra two

questions.q: What is a schema?
questions.explain: A schema is a value in your program, not just a type. It can check any real value while the program runs, and it can also give you the type through Infer.
options: A TypeScript interface that is checked while compiling
A database table with its columns and types
A description of valid data that exists at runtime, and checks real values
A JSON file that lists all the routes of an API

questions.q: What does type NewTask = Infer<typeof NewTaskSchema> give you?
questions.explain: You describe the data once. The schema checks it at runtime, and Infer produces the matching compile-time type. Change the schema and the type changes with it.
options: A runtime check that runs every time NewTask is used
The TypeScript type made from the schema, so the check and the type can never disagree
A copy of the schema that accepts any value
A JSON example of a valid task

questions.q: The title rule is schema.string().trim().min(3).max(100). Why does the title " " fail?
questions.explain: The steps run in order. After trimming, " " is an empty string, so .min(3) refuses it. Without .trim(), three spaces would pass as a title.
options: Because a string of spaces is not a string
Because .trim() throws an error on empty strings
Because titles may not contain spaces at all
.trim() runs first and makes it "", which is shorter than 3 characters

questions.q: What does done: schema.default(schema.boolean(), false) mean?
questions.explain: A default fills in a missing field. A value that is present must still pass the check: "sometimes" is refused, because it is not a boolean.
options: done is always false, whatever the client sends
done must be a boolean, and becomes false when the client leaves it out
done may be any value, and is converted to a boolean
done must be sent, and false is its only allowed value

questions.q: What does NewTaskSchema.parse(value) return when the value is good?
questions.explain: parse gives back new, clean data. That is why you use its result, not the original input. { success, data } is what safeParse returns.
options: The same object you passed in, unchanged
A clean copy that matches the schema: trimmed, with defaults filled in

questions.q: Inside an API, where bad data means "stop here", which method is the usual choice?
questions.explain: parse stops the work at once with a SchemaError, which is already a 400. A type assertion checks nothing at runtime, so it would let bad data through.
options: parse, which throws a SchemaError on bad data

questions.q: When should you use safeParse instead of parse?
questions.explain: safeParse never throws. It returns { success: false, issues }, and you decide what to do with each issue.
options: When the data comes from your own code and is always correct
When you want to look at the problems yourself, without an exception
When you want the check to be skipped in production
When the schema has default values

questions.q: Each issue has a path, a code and a message. Which one should your code check to decide what went wrong?
questions.explain: The message is written for people and may change. The code is a stable word for programs. The path tells you where, not what kind of problem.
options: message, because it is the most detailed
code, such as invalid_type, which is meant for code to check
None of them; count the issues instead

questions.q: In TypeScript, after if (!result.success) { … }, what does TypeScript know?
questions.explain: safeParse returns a discriminated union, like the Result type from Generics. Checking success narrows it: issues when false, data when true.
options: Nothing: you must cast with as to read the result
That the value is always a string

questions.q: A client tries to create a task with a title that already exists. Which error should the service throw?
questions.explain: The input is well-formed, but it clashes with what already exists: that is a 409 Conflict. A 400 is for data that breaks the schema, and a 404 is for something missing.

questions.q: Why does TaskService.create take input: unknown instead of input: NewTask?
questions.explain: The input may come straight from a request body. Typing it unknown forces the service to check it before use; parse then gives back a real NewTask.
options: Because unknown makes the code run faster
Because NewTask cannot be used as a parameter type
It does not trust its caller: it checks the input itself with the schema
Because unknown turns off the schema's checks

questions.q: In respond, what does error.expose tell you?
questions.explain: Errors like NotFoundError have messages written for clients. When expose is false, the message may hold internal details, so it must not be sent.
options: Whether the error has a stack trace
Whether the error's message is safe to show to a client
Whether the error was already logged

questions.q: An unexpected error (say, a bug that throws a TypeError) reaches respond. What is the safe answer?
questions.explain: You never send internal details, such as a stack trace or a database message, to the outside world. The client gets "Something went wrong"; your logs keep the rest.
options: Status 500 with the error's stack trace, to help the client debug
Status 200 with an empty body, so the client does not worry
Status 500 with a generic message, keeping internal details on the server
Status 400, because every error is the client's fault

questions.q: The service throws errors. Where are they turned into a status code and a JSON body?
questions.explain: The service only throws the right error. One place at the edge maps every error to a status and body, so the rules never mix with HTTP.
options: Inside every service method, before it throws
At the edge, like respond; later lessons let the HTTP layer do it
In the schema, when it checks the input
In the client's browser, which reads the error class

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An enum accepts only the exact words listed, so "HIGH" in capitals is refused. A word that is not in the list gives the code invalid_enum; it is still a string, so it is not invalid_type.

questions.q: A default fills in a missing field. What does this print?
questions.explain: A missing done gets false. A real true is kept, not replaced by the default. And "yes" is present but not a boolean, so it is refused: the default never hides bad data.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: parse does not change your input. It returns a new, clean copy, so always use the value it returns.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: safeParse always returns an object and never throws. On success it holds data; on failure it holds issues. Check success first.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each class brings its HTTP status and a stable code string that clients can check. You only write the message.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: parse throws before "created" is printed. The SchemaError is already a 400 Bad Request; the details of each problem are in its issues, not in the message.
options: SchemaError 400 String must be at least 3 characters

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A NotFoundError is exposable, so its message is sent. The TypeError is not a BaseError, so the client gets only a generic 500 and never sees the internal message.
options:
{"status":404,"body":"Task 99 not found"}
{"status":500,"body":"secret.split is not a function"}

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: " Buy milk " is trimmed to an existing title: 409. "no" is too short: 400. Both fail before nextId changes, so "Walk dog" gets id 2.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both problems are reported at once, so a client can fix everything in one go. done is missing, but it has a default, so it is not a problem.
options: false title and done and priority

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A default only fills in a field that is missing. null is a value, and it is not a boolean, so it is refused with an issue at the path done.

questions.q: A client adds a field the schema does not know. What does this print?
questions.explain: The clean copy holds only the fields the schema describes. ownerId and isAdmin are dropped, so a client cannot sneak them into your task.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ZudoJS client errors like 404 and 409 have messages meant for clients, so expose is true. A plain Error has no expose at all, which is why respond treats it as a generic 500.

questions.q: Write NewTaskSchema: title a string, trimmed, 3 to 100 characters; done a boolean that defaults to false; priority one of "low", "normal", "high", defaulting to "normal".
questions.explain: Chain the string rules with .trim().min(3).max(100), and wrap a schema in schema.default(…, value) to fill in a missing field.

questions.q: Finish problems(body). Use safeParse. Return an empty list for good data; otherwise return one string per issue: "PATH: MESSAGE", with the path joined by ".".
questions.explain: Check result.success first. On failure, result.issues holds one issue per problem; map turns each into a readable line.
questions.expected:
[]
[
  'title: Expected string, received number',
  'done: Expected boolean, received string'
]

questions.q: Finish get(id): return the task, or throw a NotFoundError with the message Task ID not found.
questions.explain: Map.get returns undefined for a missing id. Throw the ready-made NotFoundError; it brings the 404 and its name with it.
questions.expected:
Buy milk
NotFoundError 404 Task 99 not found

questions.q: Finish create(input): parse input with NewTask; if a task with the same (trimmed) title exists, throw a ConflictError; otherwise store { id, ...data } with the next id and return it.
questions.explain: Parse first, so the title is trimmed before you compare it; " Buy milk" then clashes. A bad title makes parse throw a SchemaError before anything is stored.

questions.q: Finish respond(action). Call action() and answer { status: 200, body: result }. If it throws a BaseError whose expose is true, answer { status: error.statusCode, body: { error: error.code } }. Anything else: { status: 500, body: { error: "ERR_INTERNAL" } }.
questions.explain: Every outcome becomes a status and a body. The plain Error gets a generic 500, so the internal database address in its message never leaves the server.

questions.q: This is TypeScript. Create the type NewTask from the schema with Infer (do not write an interface by hand), and finish describe so it returns "TITLE (PRIORITY)".
questions.explain: type NewTask = Infer<typeof NewTaskSchema>; makes the type from the schema. The value that parse returns has exactly that type, with the default already filled in.

questions.q: This is TypeScript. Finish titleOrError(body: unknown) with safeParse: return the clean title on success, or "invalid: " followed by the first issue's code on failure. No type assertions (as) needed.
questions.explain: Checking result.success narrows the union: inside if (!result.success) TypeScript knows issues exists, and after it, data is typed from the schema. (With strict settings, issues[0] may be undefined, hence ?..)
questions.expected:
Buy milk
invalid: too_small
invalid: invalid_type

questions.q: Finish splitBodies(bodies): check each body with safeParse, and return { valid, invalid }, the number of good and bad bodies.
questions.explain: safeParse never throws, even for null, so it is easy to use in a loop. Only "Buy milk" and "Read" with done: true pass.

questions.q: Finish createMany(inputs). For each input, call service.create(input). Collect the new task's id on success, or the error's code when it throws. Return the list.
questions.explain: Wrap each call in its own try/catch, so one bad input does not stop the others. The stable code tells your program which error happened.
